The newly hatched chick emerges with a wet weight at birth of just 9.0 grams [Wwb = 9.0 grams], a modest initial mass that is typical for altricial seabird neonates. This low birth weight belies the rapid growth trajectory that follows, driven by intensive biparental provisioning of lipid-rich stomach oil and partially digested fish. The early nestling period is characterized by a progressive shift from yolk-dependent reserves to exogenous feeding, with the chick relying entirely on parental regurgitations for its nutritional intake during the first several weeks of life.

The nestling chick remains in the burrow throughout this period, growing a dense coat of downy feathers that provides thermal insulation against the cool, damp conditions of the nesting crevice. Field studies indicate that the rate of mass gain is not linear; rather, it accelerates during the middle third of the nestling period before plateauing as the chick approaches fledging condition. The fledgling achieves its first flight after a period of intensive feather growth, during which the pin-feathers unfurl and the wing muscles strengthen through brief, increasingly long periods of wing-flapping exercise within the burrow entrance. Upon nest departure, the young bird is nutritionally independent and capable of sustained foraging, although it may continue to return to the colony site periodically.
